text: The case for clearing pavements is real: residents praise cleaner streets, and public health matters. The harder question is what happens to the trader next. How much of a day's takings survives the walk from a busy pavement to a market stall? No one has published it. #econsky

One city centre moved out more than 8,000 vendors. The mayor counts about 8,000 street vendors; architects put the city's informal traders at 250,000 to 350,000, against just over 11,000 designated market spaces. Can you plan a move without counting the people? #econsky

Cities clear street traders off their pavements, and the pavements keep filling up again. Past clean-ups "achieved initial success, only for vendors to return within weeks". Is the problem the vendor, or the plan? #econsky

Is "move up the value chain" still enough? Our article says emerging markets need a different operating system, not just more smelters: selective upgrading, regional scale, domestic demand as a buffer, and relentless diversification. #econsky

Suppliers to the world's largest EV maker reported payment cycles stretching toward 275–300 days before regulators forced a shift toward 60-day norms. Now picture a new battery-materials plant with one big buyer. Who holds the power? #econsky

What if climbing the mineral value chain makes producers more exposed, not less? In a world of aggressive vertical integrators, the higher you climb, the more you depend on the buyer's balance sheet, payment games, product specificity and mood swings. #econsky
